name: Toys Safety Regulation
evidence_rating: ex-ante only: Commission IA forecasts plus baseline data on unsafe toys; rules apply from 2030
summary: The Commission expected the new toy rules to avoid EUR 240 million to 1.2 billion a year in health damage by banning harmful chemicals, and to cut unsafe imports through a digital product passport. The rules only fully apply from August 2030, so no effects can be measured yet. As a baseline, toys made up 15% of EU dangerous-product alerts in 2024, and industry tests found most toys from third-party online sellers broke EU rules.

indicators.objective: The proposal has no LFS indicators section; the Commission will evaluate the Regulation five years after entry into force and every five years thereafter. The Regulation entered into force in January 2026 and fully applies from 1 August 2030.

indicators.indicator: Avoided health damage from banning endocrine disruptors in toys
indicators.evidence: Not measured; chemical bans apply from 2030.

indicators.objective: Fewer unsafe and non-compliant toys on the market (digital product passport, enforcement)
indicators.target_or_baseline: Industry savings EUR 13-20m/yr on inspections and EUR 2.6-3.9m/yr from digital information; costs EUR 18m one-off + EUR 10.5m/yr for the passport
indicators.evidence: Baseline only. Toys were 15% of the record 4,137 Safety Gate alerts in 2024 (second after cosmetics). Industry test purchases found 80% of 100+ toys from third-party sellers on 10 marketplaces failed EU rules (2024).

indicators.target_or_baseline: EUR 23.5-397m one-off; EUR 249-367m of products affected (of EUR 6.56bn industry turnover)

literature.citation: European Commission (2023), Impact assessment accompanying the proposal for a Regulation on the safety of toys (executive summary SWD(2023) 270), SWD(2023) 269
literature.title: Impact assessment accompanying the proposal for a Regulation on the safety of toys (executive summary SWD(2023) 270)
literature.outcomes: child health; compliance costs; market surveillance
literature.headline: Health benefits EUR 240m-1.2bn/yr from endocrine-disruptor ban alone; one-off redesign costs EUR 23.5-397m; EUR 249-367m worth of products affected; product passport EUR 18m one-off + EUR 10.5m/yr, offset by EUR 13-20m/yr inspection savings and EUR 2.6-3.9m/yr digital information savings
literature.summary_plain: The Commission expected the new chemical bans to avoid EUR 240 million to 1.2 billion a year in health damage, at one-off costs to industry of up to about EUR 400 million.

literature.citation: European Commission (2025), Safety Gate: 2024 results, Commission annual report (as summarised by UL and SGS)
literature.title: Safety Gate: 2024 results
literature.venue: Commission annual report (as summarised by UL and SGS)
literature.headline: Record 4,137 alerts in 2024; toys 15% of alerts, second after cosmetics (36%); chemical risks 49% of all alerts
literature.summary_plain: Toys made up 15% of the EU's record 4,137 alerts on dangerous products in 2024, a baseline the new rules aim to reduce.

literature.citation: Toy Industries of Europe (2024), 80% of toys bought from third-party traders on online marketplaces fail EU safety standards, TIE press release (October 2024)
literature.title: 80% of toys bought from third-party traders on online marketplaces fail EU safety standards
literature.headline: 80% of toys bought from third-party traders on 10 online marketplaces failed EU safety standards; no well-known brands tested; 2025 follow-up reported 86% of 70 toys posed direct safety risks
literature.summary_plain: An industry test of more than 100 toys bought from third-party sellers online found 80% broke EU safety rules, the problem the passport and marketplace duties are meant to address.
literature.interested_party: EU toy manufacturers' association; competes with non-EU online sellers
